## Debug session feedback (#953, maintainer, 2026-10-31)

- **A vector or string is one line** (maintainer): no children when `literal_image` shows the whole value as a string; one bit through `dout(3)`. A vector longer than the image's 256 elements shows its start and `...` and keeps its elements: nothing else shows the tail at a glance (agent).
- **Values typed in the debugger**: one function, `design::typed_literal`, for force, deposit, Set Value and break on value. The VHDL literal is tried first, so what is a literal of the target keeps its meaning (`1` of an integer is 1, `x"A5"`, aggregates). Then, for a target of a bit-like element only (an enumeration of character literals only, with `'0'` and `'1'`: `bit`, `std_ulogic`, `std_logic`, and vectors of them), the quotes are added: `1` is `'1'`, `0101` is `"0101"`, and the length has to match (maintainer for scalars; agent for vectors). No guess elsewhere: `5` for an `unsigned` could be a number or a too short vector and is refused, a `string` keeps its quotes because `character` has identifiers and any text would fit, `x` is not `'X'`, and an array of vectors takes aggregates. A breakpoint condition's literals are read by `cond.rs` and are not touched.
- **The extension asks for no force mode** (maintainer): a force is `in`, what readers see, which is what a user debugging a design means; the console keeps `-out` for the driving value, a real difference on an output port or a resolved signal. A release without a mode ends either, so nobody has to remember which it was.
- **Dotted names are what the debugger shows** (maintainer): Watch and hover, force, deposit and release answers, break descriptions and stop texts, thread and frame names, `where`. `:top:u1:s` stays accepted everywhere, as scripts and older launch files use it, and a path may start from the scope (`u_reg.q`), first from where a name is looked up, then from the top; a data breakpoint's `dataId` is an opaque id, and stays; report lines followed in #975 ("Dotted paths").
- **A Tab never picks** (maintainer): at the prompt rustyline's list mode, plus the space a shell adds after one match. The first word offers commands only (maintainer), so a bare name is typed in full; what follows a command comes from one table (`TAKES`), for the terminal and the Debug Console. In VS Code the list's first item is what Tab takes, so with several matches the first target is what they have in common, and a keybinding makes Tab open the list when none is open. VS Code's limit: with an empty word there is nothing in common, and a second Tab takes the selected item; a target cannot insert nothing (an empty `text` falls back to the label).
- **`help` in bold** goes as an output event for a client that asks for ANSI (`supportsANSIStyling`): VS Code renders ANSI in an evaluate result only with its bold class unstyled (checked in the DOM of a headless VS Code: weight 400 in a result, 700 in output). The price is an empty line for the empty result (agent).

## Debugger tools (#944, maintainer request 2026-10-31)

- **Hang report: `--hang-report`, SIGUSR1 and the console's `waits`; silent otherwise.** A testbench that simply ends is
  not an error, and a stop time is the normal end of many testbenches, so nothing is printed without the option. The
  report labels the statement a process stands at (`Process::wait_stmt`, read cold from the suspended frame); compiled
  code does not keep it, so there the label is where the process starts. Every process that can still run is listed.
- **Delta-loop report has no flag.** An `E3002` is an error, so it says all it knows: `ErrorKind::DeltaLimit` carries the
  processes of the last delta and the signals with an event in the last 16 deltas (`LOOP_WINDOW`, from the stamps kept
  anyway, computed when the error is made). A loop of more than 16 signals shows its last ones.
- **`--assert-summary` counts per innermost statement.** A failed check in a library procedure counts at the assert in the
  library, not at its caller: one report has one place, and the first message tells the callers apart. Reports disabled by
  `SetVhdlAssertEnable` do not count, as in the assert counts; `ClearVhdlAssert` clears those counts, not this table, which
  is a history of the run. Reports of elaboration are a count in the header: they ran before the option could take effect.
  Human text by default, one object with `--message-format=json`, because CI already asks for JSON there.
- **A report takes the assert lock once more, with or without `--assert-summary`.** Reports already take that lock twice;
  an atomic flag in front of it would save little where a report also formats text and prints it.
- **`--activity` is a wrapper and an observer, like `--profile`.** Without the option nothing is wrapped or subscribed, and
  `SimControl` has no new field (one moved the hot layout before). It counts runs of a process and, per signal, cycles
  with an event. Activations the kernel skips (pure clocked processes, gates) do not run, so they do not count.
- **`break assert` stops after the report, at the severity and worse.** The report is made first so that it is not lost if
  the session ends there. The console's `break assert SEVERITY` is a threshold (`error` by default). VS Code's exception
  filters are one checkbox per severity, so they are a set; the session stops at the union of both.
- **`trace x` reads the statements, not the waits.** The signals a process reads come from its statements (`Db::reads_deep`),
  because a flip-flop's data input is exactly what a sensitivity list leaves out. Elements are not followed one by one: a
  signal counts if any element is unknown. What it cannot see is printed with every trace.
- **Past values come from the wave file through `fst-reader`, read per question.** The value-change history is not kept in
  memory. `wellen` stays a test dependency: it prints to stdout from the library when reading VHDL type data.
- **The wave layout lives in the work library, `yavs-wave-layout/<top>.txt`.** It is per testbench, goes with what it
  belongs to, and is deleted with the library; a text file a user can edit or commit. WCP gives only the displayed name of an
  item: what yavs added is known by id, the rest is found by suffix, and what stays ambiguous is left out.
- **The console's commands are one table.** `help`, Tab and `docs/console-commands.inc` read `COMMANDS`, and the test
  `cli_reference_console_commands_is_current` fails when the page is stale. The `vunit_*` rows come from the help text of the
  test runner's package.

## One "did you mean" helper for every name (#949, 2026-10-31)

User rule 35: every place that takes a name suggests a near one through the one helper. It
moved from `yavs-sem` to `yavs-diag` (`yavs_diag::suggest`; `yavs_sem::suggest` re-exports it) so
the library layer, lint, coverage and the binary reach it without a dependency cycle. This
supersedes "library suggestions retain plain Levenshtein" (#894): units and libraries now use
the same measure as the semantic ones (adjacent transposition counts as one edit, abbreviations
match). Clap's own matcher is replaced too: `main::suggest_in` removes its suggestions from a
usage error and adds the helper's, for options, subcommands and option values. Diagnostic codes and
lint rule ids are numbered densely, so a well-formed id that does not exist (`E0999`, `lint_999`)
gets no suggestion, and a malformed one only when exactly one id is close. Not covered, on
purpose: environment variables (an unknown `YAVS_*` is ignored, not rejected), exclusion globs and
instance paths (patterns, not names), the two-valued `rise`/`fall`, the manifest keys of a library
index (machine written; a damaged index says to re-analyze).

## Combination coverage and inline exclusions (yavs-syntax, yavs-lower, yavs-ir, yavs-cov, CLI, #883)

- **Metric (opt in, `--cov-kind=combination`):** a requirement is a reachable state of a decision's
  inputs, two bits each: not evaluated, false, true. Reachability follows the tree: `and`, `or`,
  `nand`, `nor` on `bit`/`boolean` skip the right operand when the left decides (LRM 9.2.2), every
  other operator, `std_ulogic` ones included, evaluates both. Skipped is distinct from false and is
  never given a value. The state is the one `CoverIn` already builds for focused expression
  coverage, so nothing is evaluated extra and short-circuit is untouched; `CoverCond` counts the
  state's own counter (`CovComb`). An input with another value than `'0'/'L'/'1'/'H'` is no
  combination. Evaluated leaves that read the same object agree. A decision with a constant
  input, more than 8 inputs or more than 512 combinations has none (`W2023` when measured).
  FEC rows are unchanged and independent. Cobertura gets no combinations.
- **Inputs and order:** the leaves of the logic tree, left to right in the source, before
  optimisation; values refer to the leaf, not to a `not` above it. Only a leaf that is a plain
  name can be addressed by name; a repeated name is ambiguous and rejected; the rest by position.
  One shared reading (`covcond.rs` `Decision`) serves the lowering and the directive checks.
- **Directives:** read from the lexer's `--` comments (`yavs_syntax::line_comments`, so a `--` in a
  string or block comment is no directive), only those starting `yavs cov`/`yavs coverage`; bound
  to the construct whose first token follows the comment group (`if`, `elsif` by its keyword,
  `while`, `exit`/`next ... when`, simple assignment); a conditional or selected assignment is
  ambiguous and rejected. Resolved against the final HIR (`yavs_lower::covdir`), checked at
  analysis by `analyze` (a file that mentions `yavs` is analysed whole, not lazily from the unit
  cache, so its HIR exists), `elab` and `run`, and applied by the lowering (`LowerOptions::
  cov_directives`, in every lowering cache key). Malformed is an error, never repaired or
  partly applied; duplicates, all waived and nothing matched are warnings. No warn-and-apply mode.
- **Persistence:** the database (version 6) keeps waived combinations with raw counts, reasons and
  places, so reports never reread sources; merging a waived with a not waived copy is `E0137`.
  Identity (hash of the decision text, now without `--` comments, and occurrence) is independent
  of directives. Older databases are marked `legacy` and the exclusion report says they hold no
  record.
- **Report:** `cov report --exclusions[=json]` (and an HTML page) lists inline and file rules, with
  status applied/redundant/matches nothing/metric not collected; a requirement is excluded
  once however many rules match. A directive for a metric that was not collected is not in the
  database and so not in the report.
- **Not applicable / deferred:** the Python scripting API (#132) does not exist yet; the VS Code
  extension has no coverage settings. (maintainer, 2026-10-30, #883 plan; defaults of the plan
  comment taken.)

## A run ends with its parent through standard input (#940, 2026-10-31)

- **`yavs run --exit-on-stdin-close`; `vunit-yavs` passes it to every run but `--yavs-interactive`.** The
  runner's `Process` keeps a pipe to the child's standard input and never writes to it, so the pipe closes when
  the runner dies by any means, SIGKILL and TerminateProcess included, on Linux and Windows alike. Rejected: a
  process group kill (does not cover SIGKILL), `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` and a parent pid poll (Unix only, `unsafe`
  or polling, and the signal follows the creating thread, not the process), a Windows-only job object. Cost:
  the design cannot read standard input in such a run; waveform and coverage files are not finished (status
  130, as a second Ctrl-C). Standard input is diverted: the watcher gets a private duplicate and fd 0 and the
  Win32 handle point at the null device (`yavs_vhpi::divert_stdin`, as `divert_stdout`), because a blocked
  synchronous read of the pipe made `GetFileType` on it hang in an embedded Python's start-up on Windows
  (CI, 2026-11-01). Not covered: a viewer that `--surfer` started keeps running. The VS Code extension
  needs nothing: it uses `--dap=stdio`, whose stream ending already ends the session. (maintainer request, #940.)
- **Foreign scalar copy-back (#937):** `ForeignArg::ScalarRef` carries the formal's base type and its static
  `(low, high)` (none when the bounds are known at run time: the base type's range then applies), so an `out`
  or `inout` scalar is checked like the elements of arrays and the fields of records.
- **Array elements and record fields (#976):** `ForeignRef::ranges` holds, per argument, the static
  `(low, high)` of the element subtype (arrays) or of each field's subtype (records), so their copy-back is
  checked against the subtype too, not only the base type. VHPI model arguments keep the base-type check.

## Dotted paths (#975, maintainer, 2026-10-31)

- **Every path yavs writes itself is dotted, through one helper, `yavs_diag::dotted`** (maintainer): `Process tb.stim`, `tb.gen(1).u.p`. Reports, runtime errors, diagnostics, `--print-hierarchy`, `--hang-report`, `--activity`, `--profile`, coverage reports and rows, wave notes, the debugger. Breaking for scripts that parse report lines; colon paths stay accepted wherever a path is typed, as older scripts and exclusion files use them.
- **Only LRM values keep colons** (maintainer): `'path_name`, `'instance_name`. The `{i}` of `SetVhdlAssertFormat` is the same kind of value inside the report's own text (maintainer): `'instance_name` of the region around the process, without the last colon, as sim1 (#982; sim2 has no `SetVhdlAssertFormat`, sim4 not run). So do VHPI names (`vhpiFullNameP`), whose users look objects up by them.
- **The kernel holds the dotted names, made once by the elaborator** (agent): reports, errors, E3002 labels and the hang report print what the kernel has, so no text can be missed and a report costs no conversion. The elaborator builds them with `.` in the first place (`Hier::dotted_in`), not by converting a colon string: a conversion per process and signal cost 15 percent more instructions on a design of many small instances that prints nothing. `Elaborated::proc_name` and `Hier::path_name` stay colon: LRM values and the debugger's keys. The nesting depth that orders processes comes from `yavs_diag::depth`, which reads either form, so the order does not change.
- **JSON is dotted too** (agent): JSON is read by scripts that feed the path back into a filter or a console, and it holds the same names as the text; a second form would mean two names for one thing.
- **For-generate indices stay as they are**: `gen(1)` is one level, in parentheses as in `'path_name`. A separator inside an index or an extended identifier is part of the name (`gen(':')`, `\\a.b\\`), which the helper knows.
- **Kept with colons, not shown**: a data breakpoint's `dataId` is an opaque protocol id; the coverage database stores `:tb:u` because the colon tells an instance from a package (`work.pkg`) and older databases stay mergeable; reports show `Key::shown`.
- **The tools normalise, the comparison stays exact** (maintainer): `tools/difftest` turns a yavs process path into `:tb:p` (`lrm_path`) before comparing, on the path field only; message text, where `'path_name` values appear, is compared as printed.

## The GitHub Action lives in its own repository (#862, maintainer, 2026-11-01)

- **`ru551n/yavs-action`, not `setup/action.yml` in this repository** (maintainer): `action.yml` at its root, versioned on its own (`v1.0.0` and a floating `v1`), independent of yavs versions. This repository only links to it.
- **`latest` is the highest release tagged `vX.Y.Z`** (agent): every yavs release carries GitHub's pre-release mark and the repository's "Latest" release is another product's, so neither GitHub mark can say what is stable.
- **No cache** (agent; the issue's plan had one): an archive downloads in seconds, and restoring from a cache would skip the checksum and leave CI testing only the restored path.
- **Levels** (rule 32): the action only installs a release. The CLI, the VS Code extension and the Python scripting API have nothing to add; `vunit-yavs` finds `yavs` on `PATH` as before, and the action's CI runs it.

## Bug priority and the documentation gate (user, 2026-11-01)

- **Compiler and simulation bugs come first** (user): a bug that affects the direct result of a simulation is fixed as soon as possible, ahead of everything; the order is wrong results, then compiler bugs (valid code rejected, invalid accepted, internal errors, crashes), then the rest. A simulator's users rely on its results above all else. `AGENTS.md` rule 26.
- **Documentation is a required gate, like tests** (user): a user-facing feature or change is not done or closed until the user guide covers it, the docs build passes and its examples were run, and the report names the pages changed or why none applies. A feature nobody can find or follow is not finished. `AGENTS.md` rule 27.
- **Openness and honesty are the general policy** (user): the README and the documentation state gaps, failures, slower cases and pre-release status plainly, so a reader can trust the rest. The performance page keeps saying where yavs is slower, and the README keeps its pre-release sentence and its links to the known limitations and the conformance report. `AGENTS.md` rule 28.
## Outside contributions (maintainer, 2026-11-01)

`CONTRIBUTING.md` holds the rules for people outside the project. Maintainer decisions unless marked:

- **Pull requests are welcome, issue first:** small fixes go straight to a pull request; anything larger opens an issue, so nobody builds something that gets declined.
- **Inbound = outbound:** contributions are under MIT OR Apache-2.0, at the user's option, in the standard Rust wording. No DCO, no CLA.
- **AI tools are allowed,** and agents read `AGENTS.md`. The person who submits has run the checks and can explain the change. No disclosure required.
- **Contributors run open-source checks only;** CI covers the rest. A maintainer runs reference simulator comparisons on request and checks new expected outputs then.
- **Usage questions go to GitHub Discussions;** issues are for bugs and planned work. Security problems are ordinary issues: no `SECURITY.md`, no email address.
- **Outside pull requests are squash merged;** the maintainer edits the final message.
- **Agent-only rules such as claims do not apply to human contributors.** Which rules count (agent): pushing to `main`, claims and module ownership, commit identity, host limits, as `AGENTS.md` now says.

## Conditions of `wait until` and `assert` (yavs-lower, CLI, #1020, 2026-11-01)

- `wait until` is a `condition` site (`Fx::wait_cond`): it costs what an `if` costs, and nothing about
  when it is evaluated changes, since `wait_edge` is already off under coverage. `wait_level` stays:
  it only takes one input, which has no rows.
- `assert` has its own kind, `--cov-kind=assert` (`LowerOptions::cov_assert`, `Fx::assert_cond`), with
  ordinary `Kind::Condition` rows. Why apart: rows of the false result are hit only by a failing run, so
  at most half can be hit on a passing regression and a `condition` gate would drop on working code;
  testbench assertions are also the most evaluated conditions, so the cost is the user's choice.
- An edge test in a `wait until` has no rows (`CovCond::consts` marks it, as a constant input): edge
  triggers stay on under coverage, so a clocked process never evaluates it false.
- No combinations at either: the directives bind to the decisions they know, which are unchanged.
- The rows of a wait and of an assert hash their site's word with the text (`collect`). Occurrences are
  numbered per kind and hash over what was lowered, so sharing the hash with an `if` of the same text
  would shift that `if`'s occurrence in a run with `assert` on, and a merge with a run without it would
  silently add the `if`'s counts to the assert's row.

## State machine exclusions in the source (yavs-lower, yavs-cov, CLI, #1020, maintainer 2026-11-01)

- `-- yavs cov exclude state NAME` and `transition FROM -> TO` stand before the `case` on the register or a `when` of it (maintainer): the placement names the register, so the directive holds no signal. They apply in every instance, like other directives.
- A `when` is recognised by the next token being that word and the smallest statement around it being a `case`. The HIR has no span for the keyword, and a `when` in a conditional assignment has that assignment as its smallest statement.
- The check calls `yavs_lint::machines` from `covdir`: a new `yavs-lower` to `yavs-lint` dependency, so there stays one reading of what a machine is. Lint only needs `yavs-sem`, so there is no cycle. It runs only for a file holding such a directive.
- The states are checked against the type. A pair no alternative assigns is `W2022`, and the waiver is still kept: a transition no alternative names, such as a reset, comes into the database when it happens, and the directive excludes it there, as an exclusion row would.
- Excluding a state does not exclude its transitions (maintainer), same as rows.
- Database version 13 (state machine lines gain process and waivers), since the waivers must merge with `E0137` like others. 12 is still read.
- Rows and regions: a `process` row takes a machine through the process that holds its `case`. In a two-process machine, that is not the clocked one. `-- coverage off` around the register or around every `case` on it takes the machine, around a literal or assignment that state or transition. Toggles stay as they were: regions do not reach them. `unit` rows name packages and never reach these items.

## State machine coverage (yavs-cov, yavs-lint, CLI, #1020, 2026-11-01)

- **A kernel observer, not counters in the code** (`yavs_cov::fsm`, as toggles): it compares the
  register's value with the last one, so every tier and thread count sees the same, and lowering and
  the optimiser are not touched. A self-loop changes no value, so it is not an item.
- **One detection** (maintainer, 2026-11-01): `lint_710`, `lint_711`, the `state_machines` of `--facts` and
  `--cov-kind=fsm` all read `yavs_lint::machines` (`design/fsm.rs`), one implementation and one walk. A
  machine is a register: a signal of an enumeration type declared anywhere but `std` and `ieee`, driven
  by a clocked statement, selected on by a `case`. Compared with the rules' earlier reading, per type and
  only for a type of the architecture:
  - **Wider:** two-process machines (a next-state signal a clocked statement copies into the register,
    `next <= state` holds), types of a package, a clocked concurrent assignment, and `when A | B`/`others`
    in the transitions of the facts.
  - **Per register:** a literal another signal of the type receives no longer counts as entered, and two
    machines of one type are judged apart. A `lint_710` names the register, and a type of a package
    reports at the register rather than the literal.
  - **A default that holds is no exit:** `next <= state` before the `case` keeps `lint_711` on, because
    the machine stays; a default that is a state is still the exit.
  - **Narrower, on purpose:** a literal outside the register's subtype is no finding of `lint_710`; a type
    whose `case`d signal is not itself clocked, only another of its signals, is no machine.
  - **Facts:** one entry per register rather than per type, with `register` and `readable` added; schema version unchanged, since the old keys stay.
  - **On real code** (2026-11-01, every library of the 43 realbench designs, 327 in all, none unread): the 4 findings of the
    old reading stay. 2 are new, both real: `dstruct_stack.vhdl` declares a `WAITING` state nothing assigns;
    `cache_cpu.vhdl`'s `UNKNOWN` is a deliberate trap only reset leaves, which is what `lint_711` says to waive.
    Both rules are off by default, so `tools/corpus/lint.expected` is unchanged.
  - `readable` is what the rules need and a count does not: every assignment to the register and its next
    state gives a literal or copies another of them, none comes from a port map, a parameter or a subprogram.
- **`yavs-cov` depends on `yavs-lint`**: one edge, no cycle (lint knows nothing below sem). `yavs_lint`
  still runs no rule during a run, and only with `--cov-kind=fsm` does the detection run at all.
- **Transitions no `case` names** (a reset) are added when they happen rather than dropped: every
  transition taken is in the database, at the price that such an item can only be hit.
- **What is not measured is recorded**: `W0120` at the run and `Database::unmeasured`, so a report does not
  hide a gap from whoever reads it later. Display only: not part of any total.
- Database version 10: `f0`/`f1` lines and `unmeasured` lines; older versions still read.


## Release waits for the conformance run of its tag (#1017, 2026-11-01)

- **Decision (agent, following the user policy that user-facing bugs are fixed at once; the maintainer left the choice between "stop the release" and "document that it does not"):** `release.yml` has a `conformance` job that `publish` needs. On a tag it polls (`tools/release/conformance_gate.py wait TAG SHA`) for the `conformance.yml` run of that tag on that commit, up to 15 minutes for it to appear and 130 for it to finish, and fails unless it succeeded. That run regenerates the report at the tagged commit and, only on a tag, fails when the committed `docs/conformance.md` differs (and when the cocotb regression fails, which also blocks the release). A run on `main` is no evidence: it succeeds with a warning when the report is stale (`continue-on-error`), so the gate looks at runs with event `push` and branch equal to the tag only.
- Why wait instead of re-running the check inside `release.yml`: the conformance run needs the corpora and a release build, about 10 to 40 minutes; the tag run exists anyway and runs next to the release builds.
- A failed gate leaves the tag in place and publishes nothing; the next patch version follows (RELEASING.md). A dry run (`workflow_dispatch`) only lists the conformance runs of the commit, since no tag run exists to wait for.
- Evidence: against the real runs, the gate refuses `v0.11.0` (its tag run failed, the main run of the same commit was green) and passes `v0.10.0`. Not exercised by a real tag; the first release shows the Actions side (the `actions: read` permission, the tag-run lookup).

## Conformance runs nightly (CI, #1033, 2026-11-01)

- **Decision (maintainer, 2026-11-01):** "conformance does not need to be run on every push, it can run nightly". `conformance.yml` has no trigger on pushes to `main` and no `paths` filter. It runs nightly at 04:41 UTC on `main`, on a release tag and by hand (`gh workflow run conformance.yml --ref main`, which RELEASING.md uses for the report of the exact release commit; the run's `headSha` is checked).
- A red nightly opens an issue labelled `conformance-nightly`, or comments on the open one, with the run link (the `report` job, `issues: write` on that job only), because nobody watches a scheduled run. It is not required for merging and was not before. The nightly always runs: skipping an unchanged `main` was left out to keep the workflow small.
- Consequence: a commit that makes the committed `docs/conformance.md` stale is noticed at the next nightly (a warning in the run, not an issue) or by the tag run (a failure); a release still needs a current report first (RELEASING.md step 1). The release waits for it: see "Release waits for the conformance run of its tag".

## Size of the compilation cache (yavs-cache, #1027, 2026-11-01)

Replaces the 96 entries and 512 MiB of "Compilation cache" and "Entries per directory", the 4096 objects of "Compiled
code in the compilation cache" and the 512 notes.

- **The limit is bytes: 4 GiB of entries per library directory** (`MAX_BYTES`), with `MAX_ENTRIES` 65536 as a guard on the
  directory only, 16384 objects (256 MiB unchanged) and 16384 notes. A testbench of a big suite takes about 10 MB, so this
  holds about 400. With the 256 MiB of `obj/` and 512 MiB of `units/`, a library directory holds at most about 4.75 GiB, soft
  by what parallel runs write in the 5 s between two looks. A suite only takes what it uses. No option: nobody has asked to
  move it, and a suite over it can be split into libraries.
- **Why the old limit had to go.** Measured on a suite of 122 testbenches in one library (`docs/STATUS.md`, "Size of the
  compilation cache"): it needs 655 entries and about 1.2 GB, so both the entry limit and the byte limit churned. Every warm pass
  wrote and removed entries it was about to need.
- **What goes at the limit:** first entries unused for an hour (`STALE_AFTER`), oldest first, which is what an edit leaves
  behind. Then entries unused for 10 s (`IN_USE`), most recently used first. With neither, the new entry is not stored; a new
  version of an entry that is there always goes in. A suite runs through its designs in order, so removing the least recently
  used removes each entry just before its next use. Most recent first gives up the design that just finished and keeps the
  rest; the 10 s keep the entries of the running design for its next test case.
- **Rejected: refusing every new entry at the limit.** It never evicts, but a design that does not fit loses the reuse between
  its own test cases, which a first run depends on: at 2.3 times the limit the first run cost 19 percent more instructions and
  later runs were 15 percent over the policy above.
- **Known gap:** about six times over the limit, later runs cost 7 to 8 percent more instructions than the first, so split such a suite into libraries. Measured and explained in "A suite far over the limit" (#1034). The window counts wall time, so what is removed moves with load.
- **A put looks before it writes**, so a refused entry costs no write, and the `.swept` marker holds "full" until the next look,
  so a full directory is not listed by every put.


## Coverage kinds are opt in (#1020, 2026-11-01)

- **Decision (maintainer, 2026-11-01):** "none should be on by default, all should be opt in", and the kinds are chosen with
  letters: `yavs run --cov=LETTERS` turns coverage on and selects kinds, `s` statement, `b` branch, `c` condition, `e` expression,
  `t` toggle, `f` fsm, `a` assert, `m` combination, in any order, a repeated letter harmless (`--cov=sbt`). `--cov-kind=LIST` stays
  as the long form with words and also turns coverage on. The letters are yavs's own; the table lives in `crates/yavs/src/elab.rs`
  (`COV_LETTERS`) and, mirrored, in vunit-yavs, whose test compares the two.
- **No fallback:** bare `--cov`, `--cov=`, a letter that is none, `--cov=` together with `--cov-kind`, and `--cov-file` or
  `--cov-embed-sources` without coverage on are `E0140` before analysis (exit 2). The first lists every kind with its letter and a
  command to copy; a bad letter also says the database goes in `--cov-file`, so an old `--cov=FILE` command gets its fix. An unknown
  word in `--cov-kind` keeps clap's value error with the shared "did you mean". There is no `all` shorthand.
- **The database path moved** from `--cov=FILE` to `--cov-file=FILE` (default `yavs.ycov`). This is a breaking change for every
  caller: tests, CI, the vunit-yavs interface (`--cov-file`, with `--cov-kind` or `--cov=LETTERS` from `yavs.cov_kind`,
  `--yavs-cov-kind` or `--yavs-cov=LETTERS`; a simulation with coverage on and no kind fails before yavs starts, naming the sim
  option and both flags).
- The VS Code extension and the CI action have no coverage input in this repository: `--cov` with a debug session stays `E0199`.


## Kernel cost per delta: attribution, and no fix passed its bar (#1049, lane E of #1046, 2026-11-01)

Written by Claude. Base 383ac32e, Cranelift `--tier=auto`, the windows of `tools/realbench/window.py`, instructions per delta by symbol against sim1 (sim1's counts over yavs's delta count; its own delta count was not taken), `tools/stepcount` for exact lines.

- **Bar, fixed before any code:** instructions down at least 5 percent on at least two of `sc5_fifo_repack`, `sc5_timestamp`, `hdlm_lfsr`, `fletcher_bufferreader`, `fletcher_bufferwriter_512`, none up over 1 percent.
- **Where the gap is, instructions per delta, yavs against sim1:** cycle layer 1248 and 733 on timestamp, 3416 and 2505 on the reader, 19531 and 7802 on the writer. On `sc5_fifo_repack` (12117, 10968) and `hdlm_lfsr` (1624, 1289) the kernel is near level and the excess is process code. The share of kernel in cycles did not by itself mean the gap was there: sim1 spends similar amounts in its own run time.
- **Causes ranked, ceiling then estimate of a fix, percent of the test's total:** wake and finish pass per changed signal (ceiling 14 to 32, estimate 1 to 3, the lines are flat after earlier rounds); fixed cost per delta (timestamp 11, 5; others under 2); bit drives from compiled code (`sc5_fifo_repack` 8 to 12, 4 to 5; `hdlm_lfsr` 7.7, at most 4.5); the clock edge path (timestamp 13, 5; `hdlm_lfsr` 4, under 2); wide planes compared at commit and at finish (writer 20, 3 to 7; reader 3, 1).
- **Verdict: killed before coding.** No candidate reaches the bar on two tests. These are estimates from counted lines, not measured prototypes, and `hdlm_lfsr` could not decide a 5 percent bar anyway: identical runs differ by up to 12 percent (#673).
- **Next, if a single test bar is accepted:** wide planes (writer), then fixed delta and clock edge cost (timestamp and small clocked designs).

## Cranelift code in huge pages (yavs-clift, #1046, 2026-11-01)

- **Decision:** on Linux x86_64 the machine code of every Cranelift JIT of a process goes in one 2 MiB-aligned reservation, bump allocated in compile order, a chunk made a transparent huge page once it holds 256 KiB (`hugearena.rs`; the zone logic moved out of LLVM's `arena.rs` into `yavs_llvm::hugezone`). Measured against 383ac32e on `perf/iterative`, whole runs, `--tier=auto`, 3 rounds interleaved on one core, medians. Bar set first: iTLB down at least 80 percent on GRLIB and Microwatt, cycles up on none of the nine tests.
- **Result:** iTLB misses GRLIB 0.429 to 0.043 per 1000 instructions (-90 percent), Microwatt 0.394 to 0.049 (-88); instructions 1.003, 1.000. L1i and branch misses do not move (GRLIB 0.951, 1.014; Microwatt 1.020, 0.963): this removes the iTLB gap to sim1, not the L1i or branch gaps. Peak memory level with all code compiled (721 MB both on GRLIB), cold CPU seconds level.
- **Cycles are "no rise seen", not a measured gain.** The host was loaded (load 17 to 40, other agents on the same CCD): a binary against itself gave GRLIB cycles 0.830 in that sitting, and the first variant read slower in all four sittings (#1055 tracks that). So whole-run 0.898 on GRLIB and 0.662 on Microwatt are not believed. The fair comparison is the build with the arena against the same build with it off, both not first: GRLIB 0.976, Microwatt 0.982 in windows; the other seven 0.977 to 1.015, and `hdlm_lfsr` 1.046, whose `auto` differs by up to 12 percent between identical runs (#673). A quiet run may still move these by a few percent.
- **Hosts:** anything but Linux x86_64 keeps Cranelift's default provider, Windows included: its large pages need a privilege a user account does not have, and it runs as before. A limit on the address space (1.5 GiB of it could make a later allocation fail) or a refusal of the reservation or of writable and executable memory also keeps the default provider. A kernel with no huge pages, or one that refuses a collapse, leaves the arena on small pages. Nothing of this is an error; `tests/clift_hugearena.rs` runs the conditions it can set up and compares results. `YAVS_CLIFT_HUGE=0` is the measurement knob.
- **Why writable and executable at once:** protecting part of a chunk splits its huge page. LLVM's arena has done the same since #679.
- **Rejected: a second copy of the zone logic in `yavs-clift`.** It would save a small refactor and leave two to keep equal.

## Size-first Cranelift code, C-1: killed (yavs-clift, #1046, 2026-11-01)

- **Bars, set first:** kill if all compiled bytes fall under 20 percent, L1i under 15, or cycles under 5, on GRLIB and Microwatt.
- **Existing knobs give nothing.** `YAVS_CLIFT_OPT=speed_and_size` leaves the machine code byte-identical: Cranelift 0.137 treats it as `speed`. `YAVS_CLIFT_INLINE=0` and `600` are byte-identical on GRLIB, and the former on Microwatt: so no body of these designs seems to be inlined; why was not traced.
- **`LCopy` as one out-of-line call above 1 000 IR instructions** (guards, both lookups and the copy; frame-mode code only): bytes GRLIB 31.02 to 26.14 MB (-15.7 percent), Microwatt 19.63 to 17.82 (-9.2); a limit of 100 reaches only -16.6 and -11.4. L1i at `--tier=auto`, 3 rounds: GRLIB 0.983, Microwatt 0.918. Instructions 1.004, 1.026. Cycles were not decidable on this host (see above) and do not matter: two bars are already missed.
- **So the stubs and the hot and cold split that were to follow did not run**: they were conditional on C-1. The study's aim of about 0.7 for bytes needs more than `LCopy`; about 60 percent of the bytes with no IR position are register allocator output, which registers as variables (step 2 of the iterative plan) changes anyway. Revisit size work after that step.

## Frame objects in processes (yavs-ir `opt/proc_objects.rs`, `slots.rs`, yavs-interp, runtime, #1048, plan step 1, 2026-11-01)

Written by Claude. On branch `perf/iterative`, approved as a plan by the maintainer; whether it reaches `main` is the maintainer's decision.

- **What:** a composite variable of a process, of a fixed size up to 16 KiB (64 KiB a process), with no handles, made once in the declarative part, lives after the lowered frame instead of on the heap. The slot keeps `[data, desc, handle]`, the handle stays null, and the body's loads of the data and descriptor words become `AddrOf`, so a field is a constant frame offset. Signal copies follow: `opt/slots.rs` takes a `SigGather` target and a `SigScatter` source, up to 4 KiB each and 16 KiB a process (it was 256 bytes and 4 KiB).
- **Size known from the lowered code or the instance:** the choice and the offsets come from the lowered code alone, before the walk, so the shared code and a specialised copy agree (`Machine::specialise` keeps these bytes). A variable whose size a generic sets stays on the heap in the shared code; the copy places it from the facts of `opt/decl.rs` (`Func::moved`), and the switch moves its bytes, repoints the words and frees the object. A switch is refused, leaving the process on shared code, if an object does not have the size the copy was made for.
- **Off where someone else looks:** under a debugger (`keep_variables`) and external variables (VHPI, `--wave-variables`) nothing moves, so they read what they always read. `YAVS_NO_PROC_OBJECTS=1` turns it off; it is in `opt::fingerprint`.
- **Reaching a frame object from a callee:** with plain frame addresses a frame-mode procedure used the interpreter's lookup for an address in the root frame, 25 percent more cycles for a process passing a record to a procedure that may wait. Now the address names the object: Cranelift code decodes it inline (`Gen::frame_object_try`, one test on the way to any other unknown address) over `TierFrame::root_slots`, and `Mem::find` does the same.
- **Length tests:** the #1005 checks stay in the IR at assignment. An address of a frame object is bounded by its object, not the frame, wherever it goes: its frame index holds the flag `FRAME_OBJECT`, the object's start and length, and its offset counts from the start. `slots_of` hands out only those bytes, so every path of the interpreter, a native, and a callee's `Mem::find` and `Mem::region` stop at the object as they do for a heap object (`an_offset_past_a_variable_in_the_frame_is_an_error`). The length has 8-byte steps, so up to 7 bytes of padding are inside. The IR keeps plain `AddrOf Frame`: only the value differs, and a compiled tier that makes the plain address (the LLVM generator) still reaches the same bytes, bounded by the frame. In a process's Cranelift code a constant offset inside the object has no test, and a run-time offset gets one compare (`Known::FrameObj`). The fused interpreter slot operations take constant offsets: the optimiser folded them from the type's layout, inside the object.
- **Promotion:** a frame object or a descriptor in a slot is never promoted to a register (`Opt::promote`): `Copy` and the logic writes reach them unseen. Found by `case_tab`; regression test `frame_objects_first`.
- **Measured, 2026-11-01, Cranelift, against merge base 383ac32e; host load 10 to 58 with other agents on the timing cores:** instructions per clock of the micros, compiled: m9 13 094 to 7 340, net of the clock 1.04x m16 (bar 2x); m15 16 761 to 12 435; a procedure that may wait taking the record 23 211 to 14 777; nested 20 519 to 16 980. At `--tier=auto`, where these stay interpreted: m9 24 966 to 17 987, m15 25 634 to 25 704, m17 28 117 to 28 201, m18 34 842 to 34 606 (0.3 percent up on m15 and m17). One more record bit statement, compiled: 114 to 19 instructions, sim1 5.6. GRLIB window instructions 0.979, Microwatt 0.981, whole Microwatt run 0.984. **The GRLIB bar of 3 percent cycles cannot be decided on this host** (#1055: band half-width 19.5 percent over 8 rounds). Readings ran from 0.87 to 1.31. Band-limited cycles: `sc5_fifo_repack` 0.995 +-3.2, `sc5_timestamp` 0.989 +-1.6, `neorv32_single_cache` 1.021 +-2.4.
- **Why fixed sizes only, and no held pointers:** later plan steps. Frames do not move during an activation, so an address stays valid; registers do not live across a suspension, so nothing holds an object's old address at the switch.

## The seam's last gather and scatter of a whole record: dropped by the maintainer (#1050, 2026-11-02)

Written by Claude. Step 5 of the iterative plan on `perf/iterative` (tracker #1046, candidates B4 and B5 of the design study #1048) kept, per plan, the last
whole-record gather and scatter of a bound plan and compared plane words and run bytes with the last ones, to skip rebuilding leaves and equal runs. Commit 4b659c0e
landed it, a revert commit on top of the branch removes it again. The maintainer dropped it on 2026-11-02.

- **Why:** the gain was under half of the estimate (estimated 10 to 15 percent of the seam; measured instructions against 383ac32e on Cranelift `--tier=auto`:
  Microwatt 0.949 and 0.983 in two sets, GRLIB 0.983), and the GRLIB `vai_window_gen_interlock` window read 1.07 and 1.22 for L1i misses, a rise nobody could
  explain. That commit's own entry had already recorded the instruction reading 0.995 to 1.069 as not attributed.
- **What stays:** the corpus tests it added, `composite/sigrec_seam` and `composite/sigrec_seam_array` (force, delayed entries, a resolved leaf, `'transaction`,
  records whose runs share bytes), guard the semantics of record signal assignment and stay. Their expected files are unchanged by the revert.
- **For anyone retrying:** the soundness argument was that a gather's leaves are a function of the plane words read now, and a run's planes of its bytes, so no stamp
  or generation for force and deposit was needed; spans that share bytes (arrays of records) must keep no image. `git show 4b659c0e` has the code.

## Cranelift: a function keeps its first route (yavs-clift, #1035, 2026-11-01)

The body of a function says how it reaches its native callees: directly (so Cranelift may inline them) or through `Mem::ntab`. The tier chose by what the policy compiled with the function, which follows the samples, so one function of an unchanged design had several bodies, each its own key and entry, read only by a run that took the same choice. Both routes run the same code, so results do not depend on it. The LLVM tier does not have this: its callees are always reached through the table.

- **Decision: under the policy, a function keeps the route it was first made with** (`cache::Routes`, a `route` entry per program): a callee the route names direct is made even when the policy did not bring it, a callee it names through the table is not called directly even when it was made. A run with no route takes the policy's choice and stores it; the first line for a function wins over parallel runs. `--tier=clift` makes every variant and has no routes.
- **Why not a route from the program alone:** calling every callee through the table loses the inlining, and calling every callee directly compiles callees the run never reaches (26 variants, 112 ms of a 120 ms compile, in `Generator::tree`'s row of `crates/yavs-clift/AGENTS.md`). A stored choice costs one small entry.
- **A wrong line cannot give a wrong result.** The entry is keyed by `yavs_llvm::program_digest` (names, kinds and sizes of the functions, as for the run-to-run profile): another program with the same digest only mis-steers calls.
- **Ceilings:** a cycle entered at another function can make a second body. A route is not improved later: if a callee becomes hot only in a later run, the function keeps calling it through the table (measured: no cost, warm instructions fell). An unchanged suite still adds functions compiled for the first time for some runs (`docs/STATUS.md` "Compiled code of an unchanged suite"), since a warm run may compile what a cold one could not pay for; this is the policy working, not a key.
- **Not taken:** one list of compiled functions per program. The list goes by name and size, so a function of another design looks like a link and is compiled outside the budget, which is half of what the store holds but pays for itself: per program, 1.9 percent more instructions cold and 1 percent warm.

## A run uses the units the library holds; a unit analysed against an earlier version is analysed again (#1053, #1054)

- **Reading.** 1076-2008 13.5 (1993 11.4): a library unit is potentially affected by a change in a unit it names, a secondary unit by a change in its primary unit, and when a unit changes "all library units that are potentially affected by such a change become obsolete and must be reanalyzed before they can be used again" (quoted from the 1993 chapter 11 text; the 2008 wording was not compared word for word). The text says the units are analysed again, not who does it, and it does not make the design an error.
- **Decision (agent, 2026-11-01; the maintainer may overrule it, see the last point).** `yavs run` and `yavs elab` analyse every file of the closure again from its source (`docs/cli-contract.md`), so an obsolete unit is analysed again before it is used, without a diagnostic. The result is the one `yavs analyze` of that file followed by `run` gives. A unit that no longer analyses against what replaced its dependency fails the run with that analysis's own error (`E1100`, `E1311`, `E1230`). Which architecture an instance `e(a)` or a configuration runs is the last one analysed under that name. A stricter tool is allowed by the text and both reference simulators reject in most of these cases (`reanalysed-unit-dependents` in `docs/design/simulator-discrepancies.md`), but an error would reject nothing yavs handles wrongly, and it would need the identity of each dependency in the library records.
- **What was wrong, and is fixed (#1054).** A file that lost a unit to a later file (`partial`) was analysed whole in a run, so its old copy replaced the current unit for the rest of the session, depending on the closure's order: stale values ran with nothing obsolete in the design. `Db::analyze_closure` now analyses only the units the index still gives a `partial` file (`drop_replaced`), and of a unit declared twice in one file only the last copy, which a unit between the copies then sees too. `yavs analyze` of a file still makes all its units current. `ClosureFile::kept` puts what a `partial` file still holds in the key of the compilation cache: analysing a file again can swap the owner of a unit with the closure's files and order unchanged.
- **Primary units share one name space.** `Manifest::take_units` took a replaced unit from the index only when the kinds matched, so an entity stayed next to the package that replaced it and `use work.p.all` found the entity (`E1104`). Any primary unit now replaces any other of that name (13.5, 12.3).
- **Effect on real suites.** Nothing is rejected that was accepted before, except a unit that only worked through the stale copy. `tools/suites/pro.py` analyses all files before it runs, which the library's own scripts do not do (they analyse each test right before running it), so `TbStream_SendGetRandom1` of AxiStream runs with the architecture of `TbStream_AxiSendGetRandom1.vhd`, which defines `TestCtrl(SendGetRandom1)` again: the library holds that one. sim1 stops on that test.
- **A unit declared twice in one file warns (user, 2026-11-02, rule 47 review).** By 13.1 the units of a file are
  analysed in textual order, so a unit between two copies is obsolete again after every analysis of that file, and
  yavs gets the last copy only by analysing it first. The parser warns `W0005` at the second copy, naming the unit,
  LRM 13.1 and 13.5; the behaviour is unchanged. The two-file form has no warning (the maintainer kept it as it is).
- **For the maintainer.** An error for an obsolete unit (as sim1 gives) stays possible: it would need a record format change, so every library has to be analysed again, and it would stop this OSVVM test and any flow that analyses everything up front.

## A suite far over the limit (yavs-cache, CLI, #1034, 2026-11-02)

Whether a warm run can be kept from being slower than a cold one at any size, with the real 4 GiB limit (`docs/STATUS.md` "A suite far over the limit").

- **Decision: no change to the store or the stages; state the bound and the advice.** At about 2.4 times the limit warm is 3 percent cheaper than cold, at 3.6 times 1 percent dearer, at 6 times 7 to 8 percent dearer. Larger suites were not run. Nothing tried closes that, and each thing tried made a measured case worse. The maintainer's goal of "never slower" is not met.
- **Why:** the first run of a suite runs a testbench's test cases one after the other, so a design that does not fit still reuses its entries for as long as it runs. A later run is ordered by the test runner from its history of run times: over five copies of the suite, 616 groups of one testbench in a row became 6280. What a design that does not fit stored is then gone before its next test case. With the runner's history switched off the same warm pass took 12653 G against 12959 G cold, 2.4 percent below; with it, 13636 G, 5.2 percent above. The store's part is doing its job: the hits are the share that fits (22 percent of the runs at about 5 times the limit).
- **Tried and not taken,** each measured:
  - A closure under a made library keeping its own entries (dropping `library_made`): 17 percent over cold at about 5 times the limit, against 5.2. Each entry is written and removed again before its next use: the shortcut is right.
  - Forgetting a note with its entry, so a design that does not fit is stored on its second run as in a first run: 5.1 percent against 5.2, no gain.
  - A read not refreshing an entry's time between 30 s and half an hour, so that what a suite reads every pass stays behind what the pass writes: 1 percent under cold at 2.4 times the limit, where the unchanged store gives 3 percent under, so it costs about 2 percent there.
  - Refusing new entries was not retried: #1027 measured 19 percent on a first run.
- **What could close it, not done:** a run that needs no entries of the design's own to be cheap (the design part of a lowering stored apart from the library, which `docs/decisions.md` "Library stages" lists as a ceiling), or a run order that keeps a testbench's test cases together, which belongs to the test runner.

## x86-64-v3 baseline of the x86_64 release archives (release workflow, `crates/yavs/src/cpu.rs`, 2026-11-03)

- **Decision (user, 2026-11-03: "Go for it. All modern cpus have avx2").** The Linux and Windows x86_64 release archives are built with `-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3` (AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, FMA, F16C, LZCNT, MOVBE), still one archive per target and no extra baseline archive. The aarch64 archive is unaffected. It supersedes the "not shippable for generic hosts" verdicts on this flag in "Measured and not taken" above (which measured writer -2.8% instructions, 1 to 2% cycles, reader level or +5% cycles): the user took the decision on the CPUs in use, not on those numbers, and no new measurement was made for it.
- **Where it is set, and where not.** Only `RUSTFLAGS` in the build job of `.github/workflows/release.yml` (a matrix entry per target). `cargo build` and `cargo install` from source, `.cargo/config.toml`, CI, the conformance and cocotb workflows and `tools/build-bench.sh` stay on the Rust default (baseline x86-64), so source users on older CPUs still work. The compiled tier is unaffected: Cranelift probes the host CPU at run time, the LLVM tier targets `x86-64-v2` (above), and the C shim of `yavs-vhpi` is not built with the flag (the `cc` crate only follows `target-cpu=native`).
- **Test of what ships.** The smoke test of the release workflow, the `vunit-yavs` job and the VS Code job already run the unpacked archive binary on GitHub runners, which have AVX2; the smoke test also greps the binary for the text of the CPU check, which is compiled in only when AVX2 is a compile-time feature, so a build that lost the flag fails.
- **Old CPUs: a check at the start of `main`.** `cpu::check` reads CPUID (`__cpuid` is safe to call, so no `unsafe` and the `yavs` crate stays under the workspace `forbid`) and, when a feature of the set is missing, writes the missing names and "build from source" to stderr and exits with status 1. `is_x86_feature_detected!` is not used: it answers true without asking for a feature enabled at compile time. It is compiled in only when `target_feature = "avx2"` is on, so default builds carry nothing; the bit decoding is a plain function with unit tests on every build. The check is the first statement of `main`, which calls the rest through an `#[inline(never)]` function.
- **Exception to rule 1 and 5 (error with a code).** The message has no code, no `--explain` and does not go through `yavs-diag`: the renderer is compiled for v3 too, so using it before the check is the illegal instruction the check exists to avoid. The text still names the cause (the missing features) and the fix (build from source, the installation page).
- **How far it protects (what was checked is in `docs/STATUS.md` "x86-64-v3 archives").** Code that runs before `main` is the loader, libc start-up and the precompiled Rust standard library, all at the baseline; the only v3 code before the check is `main` itself and the `lang_start` that calls it. Ceilings: OSXSAVE stands for "the OS saves the AVX registers" (`XGETBV` needs `unsafe`), so an OS that sets it and still hides AVX state is not seen; the compiler could use a v3 instruction in the few instructions of `main` or `check` before the test (checked by disassembly, not enforced); an emulator that reports AVX2 but does not implement every v3 instruction is not seen.
- **Amendment (user, 2026-11-03, the same day): a `-compat` archive beside the v3 one.** The "no extra baseline archive" in the first bullet is withdrawn. Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64 each get two archives per release: `yavs-<version>-<target>` (x86-64-v3, the name `yavs-action` and the install docs pick) and `yavs-<version>-<target>-compat` (the Rust default CPU, so it runs on any x86-64 CPU, with no CPU check compiled in). The suffix goes before the extension, so the exact-name match of `yavs-action` (`yavs-<version>-<target>.<ext>`) cannot hit a compat file. aarch64 stays one archive. Cost: two more release build jobs (running in parallel with the others), and a `SHA256SUMS` of 10 lines. The old-CPU message names the compat archive of this version and platform first and a build from source second; the check is still free of the renderer. The release smoke test greps the plain x86_64 archives for the check's text and fails a compat archive that has it; both are smoke-tested. The `vunit-yavs` and VS Code jobs keep testing the plain archives only.
- **Build line of `--version` (user, 2026-11-03).** `yavs --version` prints a second line, `Build: x86-64-v3, AVX2 support`, `Build: x86-64 baseline` or `Build: aarch64`, and the copyright notice moves to the third. It is chosen by `cfg(target_feature = "avx2")` and `target_arch` in `main.rs`, so it is true of the binary whatever archive or build it came from (the same condition compiles in the CPU check). The first line is byte-identical, which is all the test runner package reads (`docs/cli-contract.md` section 1). The release smoke test checks the line of each archive.
- **Archive README (user, 2026-11-03).** Every archive holds a generated `README.txt` (one template in the build job of `release.yml`: version, target, CPU variant and which archive to pick, the files, how to start, the docs link). It replaces the project `README.md`, which the archives carried before and which said nothing about the archive. The smoke test checks that the first line names the version, target and variant.

## A jump back of a process that never suspends is counted however it is reached (yavs-interp, #1087, 2026-11-03)

A loop without a wait, with an `if` without an else as the last statement (`loop n := (n + 1) mod 1000; if n = 0 then m := m + 1; end if; end loop`),
never ended in any tier: no `E3009`, a silent hang (reported for `--tier=clift`, where the run did not end after 100 s; the interpreter
was affected too, see below).

- **Cause.** The false edge of the `if` goes to a block that only holds the `Br` back to the head of the loop. `Pre::new` threads a jump
  through such a block (`thread`, "an unconditional jump costs nothing"), so the branch went straight to the head and the stepped `Br` that
  `Machine::step_out` counts (#583) was never executed. Interpreted, the loop counted only the iterations that took the other edge (one in a
  thousand here), so the bound of 10^9 jumps back was 10^12 iterations. Compiled, the code counted every jump and left at the `Br` at a
  multiple of `SPIN_CHECK`, but the interpreter resumed at the pc of the `Br` through the entry table, which the threading had pointed at the
  head: the compiled code ran one iteration, left at the same `Br` with the same count, and so on for ever (`tier_go`, `run_tier`).
- **Fix, in the predecoder, so every tier gets it.** `counted_brs` (`pre.rs`) lists the retreating `Br`s of a process that never suspends
  that jump to a block laid out before them (the set compiled code polls). `Pre::new` does not thread a jump through them and `Code::new`
  does not fuse them into the `Move` or `Store` before them (`MoveBr`, `StoreSlotBr`), so each stays an `Op::Step` that every way to it
  reaches, including a resume from compiled code. Nothing changes for any other function or process, or for the dispatch loop.
- **Paths that reach the same place.** The interpreter, `--tier=clift`, `--tier=clift-auto`, and by the same code the LLVM tier, which
  polls the same `retreating_brs` set and leaves at the `Br` the same way (not run: no local LLVM tier runs). A stop request (Ctrl-C) and the
  trim every `SPIN_CHECK` jumps leave at the same `Br`, so a threaded jump back skipped them as well.
- **Not covered (as before).** A loop whose jump back is a `CondBr` or part of a fused loop op (`CmpBrStep`) is not a `Br` and is not counted
  by any tier.

## Profile-guided release archives (`tools/pgo`, `.github/workflows/release.yml`, 2026-11-04)

Written by Claude. User ruling, 2026-11-03: profile-guided builds on all platforms in 0.14.0.

- **Decision 1 (per archive).** Each of the five archives gets its own instrumented build, training and final build on its own runner with its own `RUSTFLAGS`: x86-64-v3 and baseline are different code, and a profile is per target. The profile is made in every build and never checked in. No archive ships without one: a problem fails the job.
- **Decision 2 (the build).** `tools/pgo/build.sh OUT` builds with `-C profile-generate`, runs `tools/pgo/train.py`, merges with `llvm-profdata` from rustup's `llvm-tools` (rustc's own LLVM), and builds again with `-C profile-use`. No crate changes. Everyday performance comparisons stay on non-profile-guided builds (`tools/build-bench.sh`), and a figure says which kind of build it is from.
- **Decision 3 (the training set).** Original testbenches in `tools/pgo/train/` plus a sweep over `tests/corpus`. Reason: of the real designs measured, one is in a private repository, one needs a POWER cross compiler for its program image, and two are under licences whose effect on a trained binary the maintainer has not ruled on. Against a profile trained on real designs, on designs neither saw, the two gave the same instruction counts in `run` and `elab` to within the noise (`docs/STATUS.md`); cold analysis of big library sources gained about 6 percent against 11.
- **Decision 4 (one command, Linux).** Both builds run the same `cargo zigbuild --target T.2.17`; only the instrumented one adds `-C linker=cc`, because linking it with zig fails (`__llvm_profile_runtime: unrecognized file extension`). Measured: cargo's `-C metadata`, which goes into every symbol and so into every profile name, changes with `--target` and with the linker cargo-zigbuild configures, and does not change with `RUSTFLAGS`. `cargo build --target T` against a zigbuild final build left 56258 functions without a profile, with no warning from the compiler, and the result ran 3 to 5 percent slower than a plain build on a Linux x86_64 runner. An earlier check of this branch ("the zigbuild final build gives no warning") was that case, and proved nothing.
- **Decision 5 (the check).** `tools/pgo/check.py`, called by `build.sh`, fails the job on any function missing from the profile (the final build has `-pgo-warn-missing-function`), any mismatch warning, a profile under 1000 functions, no profile runtime in the instrumented binary, or one in the final binary. There is no threshold on missing functions: the five release jobs had 0, a build that did not fit had tens of thousands. It reads the compiler's own report, so it proves the build used the profile, not how much it gained.
- **Decision 6 (no cache in the release build).** Cargo does not see a profile's content, so a cached dependency would keep an older profile. The release build job has no rust-cache, and `build.sh` deletes its final target directory.
- **Decision 7 (tests on what ships).** After the existing smoke test each job runs `tests/corpus` on the binary of the archive: `yavs-interp`, `yavs-auto`, `yavs-auto-warm`, `yavs-clift`, `yavs-clift-auto`, at 1 and 4 threads. 1 to 2 minutes on Linux, 4 to 7 on Windows. `tools/difftest/difftest.py` finds `timeout` and `bash` by full path for it, since on Windows a bare name finds the ones in System32.
- **Decision 8 (a CI step, user, 2026-11-04).** The `corpus` job of `ci.yml` runs `train.py --check`, each case analysed and run once at `--tier=interp` (31 s locally): a compiler change that rejects a training case shows on `main`, not at a release tag. It happened once already: main's new E1101 rejected a label in `big_records.vhd`.
- **Decision 9 (measuring).** `tools/pgo/gain.py`, on a dispatch with `pgo_gain=true`, never on a tag. Held-out designs from `tools/bench/designs`, three arms in turn (plain, profile-guided, plain again as control), fresh copies of the binaries. Measured: timing the linker's output against the unpacked archive read 1.12 for analysis on Linux runners, and copies of both read 1.00; why is not established. A wall figure counts only where repeated runs agree. Results: `docs/performance.md`.
- **`elab_heavy` (user, 2026-11-04: disclosed, and out of the held-out figures).** With the first training set this held-out design took 2.3 times the instructions on x86-64-v3 and 1.6 on the baseline, and 1.79 times the wall time on a Linux runner: the loop counting overlapping sources in `collapse::ports` ran scalar in the profile-guided binary and vectorised in the plain one. To cure it `train/element_ports.vhd` was added, after reading the first 20 lines of `elab_heavy` and profiling it, so that case is not independent of it and `elab_heavy` no longer counts as held out. The case stays in training. **The cause was not found:** `-pgso=false`, `-loop-vectorize-with-block-frequency=false` and `-vectorizer-min-trip-count=2` each changed nothing on that design, and vectoriser remarks did not name a reason for that loop. So one case cures one failure, and the same loss may exist on a path no case runs. The checks made for it since: 25 other designs of `tools/bench/designs` and 34 real testbenches (instruction counts, `docs/performance.md`), none near that size.
- **Known loss, cause not established.** `rtl_bus` on the Linux `-compat` archive is 4 to 6 percent slower than plain in three runs of seven rounds each, on an AMD EPYC 9V74 where the CPU was recorded; on our own host it executes the same instructions (0.996) with cycles at 0.958 on a shared machine. The runner has no counter to look further. `ieee_heavy` on the same archive reads 1.00 to 1.02.
- **Not decided here:** whether a profile trained on freely licensed real designs should replace or join the original set.
- **Decision 10 (bench builds, maintainer, 2026-11-06).** Runtime changes are judged on profile-guided bench builds after an A/A of two such builds of one source; generated-code changes on plain bench builds by exact counts. `tools/build-bench.sh --pgo OUT [cargo args]` runs `build.sh` with the bench build (aligned functions, line tables) and `--target HOST` in both steps; a plain build it is compared with gets the same `--target`, since the flag alone moved cycles by up to 5 percent with equal instructions. Reason: a plain profile-guided build read 0.89 of the plain one in cycles on the largest design, beyond its A/A, so a runtime gain on a plain build may vanish in what ships. Method: `tools/bench/AGENTS.md` section 7.

## Registers of process code as Cranelift variables: killed at its bars (yavs-clift, #1048, plan step 2, 2026-11-02)

Written by Claude. Nothing of this is on the branch but this entry; whether the study's plan changes is the maintainer's decision.

- **Bars, fixed before: on `dctrl`, `execute1_1`, `decode2_1` forced compiled, kill if bytes fall under 30 percent, generated instructions under 25 percent, or compile time rises over 2x.** Prototype: variables for the registers live at a block start, stored only before instructions that can collect, push a frame or suspend and on resuming exits; a slow path stores its operands and reloads its definitions; entries limited to the start, resume points and loop heads. The running bodies, against the same binary with it off (bytes, generated instructions by samples, compile time):

  | process | bytes | instructions | compile |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|
  | `dctrl` (specialised copy) | 1.059 | 0.993 | 1.63 |
  | `execute1_1` (specialised copy) | 1.080 | 1.026 | 1.26 |
  | `decode2_1` | 1.095 | 0.937 | 1.32 |

  Bytes rose and instructions did not reach the bar. Limiting variables to registers live over at most 32 instructions: `dctrl` 0.980, 0.949, 0.86; `execute1_1` 1.088, 0.989, 1.13; `decode2_1` 1.042, 0.978, 1.01. Peak RSS forced compiled rose 24 and 25 percent, one run each.
- **Why, measured:** what the idea can remove is too small a share. In today's code the register array traffic, its base reloads and stack spills are 13 to 26 percent of the generated instructions of these bodies and under the byte bar. The rest is signal reads, `LCopy` and the guards in them. A variable that crosses the many cold calls goes to a stack slot: it trades an array load for a stack load, with more stack references than before (`execute1_1` 6 220 to 8 851 loads).
- **Share by IR kind, instructions / bytes, percent, today's code:** `dctrl` `LCopy` 22/16, no IR position 20/30, `SigReadScalar` 10/14, `Drive` 9/2; `execute1_1` `SigReadScalar` 32/25, no position 23/21, `LCopy` 13/6, `SigRead` 11/6, `SigVal` 2/23; `decode2_1` `SigReadScalar` 33/12, no position 18/18, `Drive` 9/1, `SigVal` 3/12. `Load` and `Store` together are at most 8 percent of instructions after step 1.
- **Terminal exits:** the kill test passes pooled and on `dctrl` (99 percent of its 319 exits, mean live 31), not per process on the live set (`execute1_1` copy 1 exit, 6 live; `decode2_1` 21 exits, 4 live). In the prototype it took `dctrl` from 1.115 to 1.059 in bytes and moved nothing else. Read in the code: after a failing check the interpreter builds the error from the instruction's operands and the frames' pcs; variables, waves, VHPI and coverage do not read registers (`Machine::error`, `Machine::trace`, `reflect.rs`, `debug.rs`). The debugger pins to the interpreter.
- **`--tier=auto`:** the three bodies and `comb` of `rec_pair` stay interpreted (`Kind::Frame`, `Tune::frame` off in a Cranelift-only build), so forced-compiled gains do not reach them. `rec_pair`, m9, m15 at auto are level; compiled 0.991, 0.971, 0.999 instructions per cycle. Nine windows, one round, simulation thread: instructions 0.995, 0.941, 0.995, 0.983, 0.996, 0.999, 0.911, 1.000, 0.944 (`grlib_leon3mp`, `vai_window_gen_interlock`, `fletcher_bufferwriter_512`, `sc5_fifo_repack`, `sc5_timestamp`, `fletcher_bufferreader`, `hdlm_lfsr`, `neorv32_single_cache`, `microwatt_coremark`). With compile threads, a later sitting: GRLIB 1.008, Microwatt 0.993, NEORV32 1.002. So the Microwatt reading of 0.944 is not confirmed. Cycles were one round on a loaded host: no verdict.
- **Not measured:** the correctness gate (the prototype did not pass its bars and is not on the branch), cold and warm guards of `run.py`, any cycle verdict, and the auto policy with `Tune::frame` on.

## Constant-shape LCopy in Cranelift (yavs-clift, #1057, 2026-11-02)

Written by Claude. On branch `perf/iterative`; whether it reaches `main` is the maintainer's decision.

- **Decision:** an `LCopy` with count and both offsets constant is lowered with its shape known (`lcopy_shape`, `Gen::lcopy_const`): constant shifts and masks, the second block only where the run has one, a plain whole-word move when the run is a whole word and no shift when source and destination sit at the same place in one block. The tests of count and block count go, because the constants settle them. `Gen::host` gets constants and removes what they prove, keeps the rest. A subprogram or a run over 64 elements still calls `yavs_rt_lcopy`, with constant arguments. `SubtypeCheck` is not touched (maintainer ruling pending). Source planes are read before any store, so overlapping ranges behave as before.
- **Rejected: narrow loads and stores for a byte, half or word run at an aligned place.** Fewer instructions, but a later 8-byte read of the plane does not forward from a narrower store, and the cycles to judge that cannot be measured on this host. **Rejected: 16-byte moves for whole blocks:** the same forwarding concern, an 8-byte store read as 16 bytes.
- **Bar, fixed before measuring:** keep if forced compiled (`--tier-heat=1,0,0`) on GRLIB and Microwatt instructions fall at least 3 percent and bytes at least 8 percent, and no test is up over 0.5 percent in instructions at `--tier=auto`.
- **Forced compiled, windows, 3 rounds, Cranelift bench builds.** Merge base `2c523cd8` (earlier rows of #1046 used `383ac32e`) plus only this change, then branch head `3bd029af` with and without it:

| | instructions | cycles, 95 percent band | bytes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GRLIB, merge base | 0.952 | 0.983 +-30.8 percent | 0.9007 (31.46 to 28.34 MB) |
| GRLIB, head | 0.951 | 0.933 +-10.4 percent | 0.8980 (31.06 to 27.89 MB) |
| Microwatt, merge base | 0.946 | 0.935 +-53.2 percent | **0.9227 (19.69 to 18.17 MB): misses the bar by 0.27 points** |
| Microwatt, head | 0.946 | 1.017 +-82.2 percent | 0.9199 (19.16 to 17.62 MB) |

- **Verdict: bar met at head; missed at the merge base on Microwatt bytes by 0.27 points; keep or kill is the maintainer's call.** The change is on the branch meanwhile. Bytes are exact: the two head counts repeated to the byte, and the head pass is by 0.01 points. Cycles decide nothing: every band holds 1.0 and any plausible gain.
- **`--tier=auto`, instructions, 3 rounds, B over A, in brackets the A/A of the same sitting at the merge base:** merge base: GRLIB 0.960 (0.993), `vai_window_gen_interlock` 1.025 (1.011), `fletcher_bufferwriter_512` 0.993 (1.009), `sc5_fifo_repack` 1.000 (1.001), `sc5_timestamp` 1.000 (0.998), `fletcher_bufferreader` 1.000 (0.993), `hdlm_lfsr` 0.999 (0.979), `neorv32_single_cache` 0.990 (1.007), Microwatt 0.985 (0.975). Split by mode, 8 rounds at head: high 17.782 to 17.787 G, low 16.599 to 16.619 G, under 0.2 percent. So the auto bar is met at head by that reading; the 3-round medians alone could not show it.

Microwatt's big processes stay interpreted, as expected, so its gain at auto is the small processes' only: 0.985 at the merge base and 0.943 at head, with 165 to 174 G between identical runs at the merge base, so its size is not established.

It keeps the `i128` form and runs as often as the constant form: 14.9 M at auto against 14.8 M on Microwatt, and 27 M in native variants on GRLIB, in the same census. A one-block test with 64-bit shifts and a call otherwise would serve it; not built, not measured.

## Compiled signal reads fixed at compile time: not kept at its bars (yavs-clift, #1058, lane of #1046, 2026-11-02)

Written by Claude. Nothing of this is on the branch but this entry; whether the cycle reading below reopens it is the maintainer's decision.

- **Bars, fixed before: keep if, forced compiled, instructions fall at least 3 percent on Microwatt or GRLIB, bytes do not rise, and no test rises over 0.5 percent at auto.** Prototype: a function with a `SigVal` tests the table length once at its entry; a `SigVal` of constants has no test of its own; the `SigReadScalar` right after it loads the entry's `codes` read-only, tests it (element 0) or `len` (other elements) and loads the byte: 5 instructions against 15. The planes and bytes forms go out of line into cold blocks, every other reader of such a reference skips its table tests, and `dst` stays in hand after the join.
- **Result, forced compiled, on 631ad5a2, one binary each, simulation thread:**

Forced compiled, signal reads are 21.4 and 9.5 percent of generated code, and generated code is about half of the window. ## Cranelift: cold continuations (yavs-clift `cold.rs`, #1046, 2026-11-02)

Written by Claude. On branch `perf/iterative`; whether it reaches `main` is the maintainer's decision.

- **Decision:** before a body is compiled, a block all of whose predecessors are cold becomes cold, and a conditional edge from a cold block to a hot block goes through a cold block of its own. Only flags and jump-only blocks change. Cranelift gives a split edge the coldness of its successor only, which is why the second half is needed.
- **Why:** a slow path's continuation (`Gen::call_go` makes it) was not marked, so it sat in the hot stream and hot code jumped over it with a taken forward conditional. A predictor that no longer knows such a branch guesses fall-through and misses. The hot path is now the fall-through.
- **Bars, set first:** on GRLIB and Microwatt branch misses per 1000 instructions down at least 15 percent, L1i at least 8, cycles at least 5 with the band excluding 1.0, instructions within 0.5 percent; no test's cycles up beyond its band; cold compile at most +3 percent.
- **Result, kept on the run-time bars; one cold compile cell undecidable (below).** Change alone on the merge base of the branch with `main` (2c523cd8), `window.py --full`, `--tier=auto`, pristine world per variant, simulation thread, core 9 or 11, CCD1 not quiet: load 6 to 40, up to five simulators on the CCD. Two copies of the base ran beside the change, so each row has two ratios and an A/A:

  | whole run | cycles, against each base, 95 percent band | A/A cycles | instructions | branch misses per 1000 | L1i per 1000 | L1i tag misses per 1000 | to sim1, cycles |
  |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | GRLIB, 6 rounds | 0.845 [0.807, 0.884], 0.878 [0.851, 0.905] | 0.962 [0.945, 0.980] | 0.997 | 0.637, 0.644 | 0.779, 0.806 | 0.809, 0.818 | 3.30 and 3.19, then 2.77 |
  | Microwatt, 4 rounds | 0.916 [0.894, 0.940], 0.873 [0.796, 0.958] | 1.050 [0.979, 1.126] | 1.000 | 0.705, 0.698 | 0.877, 0.834 | 0.826, 0.813 | 3.93 and 4.11, then 3.58 |

- **Nothing small slowed:** the nine windows (5 rounds, cycle geomean 0.964 +-3.1) have no test above its band, highest `sc5_timestamp` 1.013 +-5.2. Twelve head-to-head designs, core 8, 6 rounds: `rec_pair` 0.985 +-1.0; highest `xor_sig` 1.018 +-2.3, `compute_h2h` 1.014 +-3.6 and `rtl_chain` 1.011 +-1.1, read again on core 10 over 16 rounds as 0.994, 1.002 and 0.996. `lfsr64_xor` instructions 0.951: a compile outcome, not this layout.
- **Cold compile:** user CPU, fresh world, all compiled to 5 us, cores 8 and 10: GRLIB 1.027 [1.023, 1.032], 32 pairs; Microwatt 1.018 [1.008, 1.028], 24 pairs. Under `auto` from a fresh world, GRLIB to 300 us, 8 pairs: 0.997 [0.966, 1.028]. Microwatt and `auto` pass. **GRLIB all compiled is undecidable against the bar by 0.2 percent:** its point value is under 3 percent and the top of its band over it. The bar was not moved.
- **Results cannot change:** difftest 612 of 612 on interpreter, Cranelift, `yavs-auto` and `yavs-auto-warm` at 1 and 4 threads with the verifier on; external lists 995 and 455 pass.
- **On the branch at 3bd029af, before and after this change, whole runs:** GRLIB cycles 0.891 [0.871, 0.912], instructions 1.001, branch misses per 1000 0.68, L1i 0.76, tag misses 0.83, to sim1 3.00 then 2.67. Microwatt 0.885 [0.869, 0.900], 1.000, 0.68, 0.68, 0.83, 3.70 then 3.25. Nine windows, 3 rounds: cycle geomean 0.967 +-3.2, none up beyond its band.
- **Small designs on the branch read slightly differently:** over 16 rounds `rec_pair` 1.008 +-0.6 and `rtl_lfsr` 1.024 +-1.7 (instructions 1.009), both above their bands, where the merge base read 0.985 +-1.0 and 0.989 +-0.8. All compiled, so without tier policy, 16 rounds: `rec_pair` 0.993 +-0.5, `rtl_lfsr` 1.029 +-1.0 at equal instructions. So `rtl_lfsr` on the branch is a real layout cost of about 3 percent, and `rec_pair`'s reading follows the compile outcome. The bar was on the merge base and is judged there. Not chased.
